story: Fires where the text resumes a rhythm the document has already established, predicting a separator or continuation token that appeared earlier in the same context.
At the end of a complete descriptive sentence it predicts the closing period or the newline that follows.
Continues a boilerplate template that already occurred earlier in the document (a listing format, figure caption, or code header), copying the next token of the repeated pattern.
After a noun phrase it predicts the small grammatical word or punctuation that links it onward (is, are, and, the, or a comma).
At the end of a long noun-heavy clause it predicts the sentence-final period or clause-separating comma.
Completes the second half of a conventional hyphenated pair or range, predicting the token right after a hyphen (the end of a day range or a compound like Top-end).
Continues a word the tokenizer split mid-way, predicting the next subword fragment of an unfinished word or name.
Supplies the routine continuation of a stock phrase, usually a short preposition-like function word or the fixed lowercase suffix of a familiar sequence such as .co.uk.
Completes a split word or short alphanumeric code with its next fragment, such as the digit of a postcode-like code or the middle piece of a longer word.
Continues a multi-token proper name or technical identifier, usually echoing a name already introduced in the document.
At the point where a sentence is grammatically complete it predicts the ending punctuation or the newline.
Completes a fixed multi-token name or stock phrase with its memorized next piece (GOOG->LE, Buckingham->Palace, Stow-on->the).
Predicts the content word that completes a familiar collocation (for -> centuries, 22 -> percent, a possessive followed by its noun).
Inside compound or possessive constructions it predicts the joining punctuation, most often the hyphen of a hyphenated word.
Predicts the punctuation mark or newline that closes off the current word or clause (hyphen, comma, period), in prose and code alike.
In mid-sentence it predicts the comma or the high-frequency function word that carries the clause forward.
At the end of a short heading or label line it predicts the newline, matching the line-break pattern set by earlier headings in the same document.
During an enumeration or running clause it predicts the list comma or the function word extending the phrase.
Continues a multi-word term whose completion already appeared earlier in the document, repeating the earlier continuation.
Continues a multi-piece proper name or rare technical word, predicting its next subword fragment.
